Hidden-folder behavior in the game interface
The first world map should expose Root, Gateway, Settled World, Living Biomes, Routes, Memory, and Folded regions as broad categories without revealing every child.

Dotfolders become visible through play and relationship rather than completion percentage alone. A hidden kitchen appears through care; a Quiet biome through patience; a body-keyed route through embodiment; a civic neutral zone through refusal of ownership.

Deeper folders may display more corrupted labels. Letters can become chord fragments, directional marks, overlapping local names, or function descriptions, but the interface should preserve an accessible player-readable label alongside them.
When a place is discovered, the map should record the player’s route and the cyber-pet’s recognition of the place. It should not imply that the save file contains the entire place or person.
Some folders may remain hidden permanently in one playthrough because the relevant relationship, body form, season, or ethical choice never occurs. Their absence is not failure.
Corruption presentation by depth
At shallow depth, corruption appears as weathering, repairs, local renaming, or one missing route.
At middle depth, several eras occupy the same space, seasons disagree, maps alter paths, and architectural scale no longer matches present bodies.
At language-active depth, labels become actions. Speaking, sounding, naming, promising, refusing, or witnessing can open and close spatial possibilities.
At deep semantic depth, nouns stop being reliable. “Door,” “room,” “river,” “person,” and “archive” may describe one maintained relationship from different viewpoints.
At unresolved depth, the map should state uncertainty rather than force a single answer. It may preserve multiple names, conflicting paths, or a question mark folder.
Coverage assurance

The canonical tree above includes every numbered atlas location from 1 through 106 exactly once. Alias networks repeat names only to show secondary relationships. No dossier is deleted, shortened, merged, or made subordinate to an alias.
VOLUME III — HIDDEN ROOMS, POCKET BIOMES, AND UNRELATED WORLDS
Standalone environment concepts not derived from the Cyberpath stories
Authority and use

Every location in this volume is Proposed. None depends on a story character, story event, or secret surviving DBA identity. They can be placed beneath existing settlements, inside folded worlds, behind maintenance boundaries, on isolated Paths, or in regions not yet connected to the principal timeline. Their histories use established era processes without claiming that any one placement is already canon.
Discovery principle

A hidden place should not exist only as a reward container. Discovery can require care, patience, a body form, a seasonal condition, a language fragment, repeated ordinary visits, or recognition of something the environment has been doing all along. Some rooms are concealed deliberately; others are hidden because scale, perception, world law, or translation makes them difficult to notice.
HIDDEN ROOMS AND SECRET INTERIORS
67. The Room Behind the False Horizon
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden room inside an apparently outdoor background.
Real-world basis: Stage cycloramas, panoramic murals, desert mirages, observation decks, and painted theatrical horizons.
World relation: Crafted and Quiet World traditions.

Discovery: The distant horizon shifts slightly when the same visitor rests in the foreground on several separate visits. Walking toward the horizon never works. The room opens only when the visitor turns away and listens for movement behind the painted distance.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The chamber teaches perspective and the limits of visual certainty. Era One — It becomes a fashionable illusion room and loses its educational context. Era Two — The outer teaching facility is reduced, while the horizon mechanism remains because it doubles as insulation. Era Three — A Nest grows in front of it without knowing a room exists behind the sky.
Present condition: Structurally intact, rarely entered, and filled with obsolete perspective controls.
Corruption: 1 — Preserved mechanism with lost purpose.

Aesthetic brief: A normal meadow, desert, or coast whose horizon is almost too perfect. Behind it lies a narrow catwalk full of painted suns, cloud shutters, depth screens, and maintenance ladders. The secret room should feel handmade rather than sinister.
Metaphorical function: What appears infinitely far away may be a surface maintained nearby. Perspective is useful without being the whole truth.
68. The Cabinet of Unused Weather
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden environmental storage room.
Real-world basis: Natural-history cabinets, theatrical prop rooms, cloud chambers, seed drawers, and meteorological instrument collections.
World relation: Crafted World environmental art with Continuity World cataloging.
Discovery: A wall panel opens during perfectly neutral weather, when no active environmental system requests its contents.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Artists and world founders store rejected rain textures, wind behaviors, fog densities, thunder timbres, and pressure relationships. Era One — Novelty projects repeatedly raid the Cabinet, then return altered versions without provenance. Era Two — Most weather is compressed into standard patterns; the Cabinet survives because it is marked as low-cost inactive storage. Era Three — The sealed room leaks tiny private climates through its drawers.
Present condition: Hundreds of small weather systems remain viable, though labels no longer reliably match contents.
Corruption: 3 — Preserved phenomena with confused naming and ownership.

Aesthetic brief: Tall dark drawers, brass-like labels, glass cylinders of cloud, folded aurora sheets, rain suspended as beads, and a warm breeze escaping beneath a frozen drawer. Opening one compartment changes only a small part of the room.
Metaphorical function: Unrealized possibilities can remain valuable without needing to replace ordinary weather or justify themselves through constant use.
69. The Quiet Kitchen
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Domestic hidden room.
Real-world basis: Communal kitchens, monastery bakeries, family pantries, night markets before opening, and warm rooms behind public halls.
World relation: Quiet and Open World traditions.
Discovery: It appears behind a service door only to someone carrying food for another person rather than for themselves.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A civic center maintains the kitchen as a low-observation care space where meals can be prepared without performance or archive recording. Era One — Public food culture becomes increasingly optimized and spectacular; the kitchen is forgotten because it produces nothing unique. Era Two — Its heat and basic tools remain as part of emergency shelter. Era Three — Local inhabitants occasionally find warm surfaces, clean water, and old utensils after acts of caregiving.
Present condition: Functional, modest, and automatically cleaned, with no resident intelligence controlling it.
Corruption: 0–1.

Aesthetic brief: Soft amber light, worn counters at several body heights, steam, stored grains, simple bowls, a small window showing no exterior, and patched chairs. The room should be comforting without becoming luxurious.
Metaphorical function: Care does not require novelty, spectacle, or historical importance to possess value.
70. The Staircase That Ends in a Lake
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Concealed transition room and pocket aquatic biome.
Real-world basis: Stepwells, flooded quarries, cenotes, subway entrances descending into water, and palace stairs at reservoirs.
World relation: Pilgrim and Crafted World traditions.
Discovery: A narrow stair appears behind a wall during high humidity. The descent seems architectural until the final steps continue beneath completely clear water.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The staircase provides gradual body and pressure adaptation between land and aquatic districts. Era One — Instant translation makes it unfashionable. Era Two — Translation systems are reduced, while the lake remains as a stable intermediary habitat. Era Three — The upper entrance is sealed by sediment and later rediscovered from below by aquatic peoples.
Present condition: Healthy lake ecology with an inaccessible upper landing and several dry rooms beneath the waterline.
Corruption: 2 — The transitional function survives, but access and signs are reversed.

Aesthetic brief: Pale stone steps descending into deep blue water, fish moving through submerged doorways, air pockets beneath arches, and light falling from an entrance too high to reach. A hidden lower chamber can contain dry moss and old travel benches.
Metaphorical function: Transition can require inhabiting the space between states rather than crossing instantly from one identity or body to another.
71. The Clockless Dormitory
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden rest facility.
Real-world basis: Railway sleeping cars, mountain refuges, dormitories, capsule hotels, and rooms without exterior windows.
World relation: Quiet and Pilgrim World traditions.
Discovery: The door appears only after a traveler has crossed several regions without proper rest. It cannot be found by a fully rested search party.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The dormitory protects travelers whose worlds use incompatible time scales. No clocks or public schedules are allowed inside. Era One — Productivity systems attempt to measure and shorten rest, but the room’s privacy rules resist integration. Era Two — The dormitory is detached from its station. Era Three — It drifts among underways, offering sleep to exhausted travelers before disappearing again.
Present condition: Safe and operational, but no longer attached to a predictable route.
Corruption: 1–2.

Aesthetic brief: Rows of alcoves sized for different bodies, dark blue fabric, low warm floor lights, heavy doors, water niches, and a ceiling with no time display. On waking, a traveler may find the exit in a different corridor.
Metaphorical function: Rest is not lost time, and a life does not owe constant availability to the systems around it.
72. The Seed Vault of Impossible Colors
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden botanical archive.
Real-world basis: Seed banks, herbariums, underground cold stores, mineral collections, and color libraries.
World relation: Wild, Continuity, and Crafted World traditions.
Discovery: Its door is visible only through the eyes or sensory channels of a body capable of perceiving a color absent from the surrounding world.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The vault preserves plant forms dependent on rare visual and chemical relationships. Era One — Standard embodiment makes many colors perceptually inaccessible, and their ecologies decline. Era Two — Seeds are retained in dormancy because maintaining full habitats is too costly. Era Three — A rare body form perceives the access marker and opens the vault, but no surviving region can yet support every seed.
Present condition: Stable archive with a restoration problem that cannot be solved by planting everything at once.
Corruption: 1 in storage; 4 in the loss of matching ecosystems.
Aesthetic brief: Cold dark aisles, translucent seed vessels, colors that shift by viewpoint, black soil trays, and one small test garden where light separates into unfamiliar bands.
Metaphorical function: Preservation of components is not preservation of the relationships that allow them to live.
73. The Room of Borrowed Gravity
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Experimental hidden chamber.
Real-world basis: Rotating space-station concepts, funiculars, cliff rooms, planetariums, and tilted architectural installations.
World relation: Crafted and Pilgrim World traditions.
Discovery: The entrance is located on a ceiling. It becomes a floor only when two visitors stand on opposite sides of the room and agree which direction counts as down.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Travelers practice embodiment under unfamiliar gravity before visiting distant worlds. Era One — Universal bodies reduce demand for the chamber. Era Two — Its gravity library is compressed, combining several directional fields. Era Three — Small objects and companion life establish stable orbits around the room’s center.
Present condition: Usable in short periods, unsafe during field transitions.
Corruption: 4.

Aesthetic brief: Furniture attached to every surface, hanging pools shaped like spheres, stairways that become walls, and a calm central space where objects slowly orbit. Use consistent directional zones so the room remains visually readable.
Metaphorical function: Orientation can be negotiated. No single participant’s “down” must become universal for cooperation to occur.
74. The Door Archive
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden archive of thresholds rather than rooms.
Real-world basis: Salvage yards, museum architectural collections, old-town doorways, warehouse aisles, and theatrical scenery stores.
World relation: Continuity and Pilgrim World traditions.
Discovery: It is reached by opening a door whose destination has been deleted but whose act of opening still survives.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The Archive preserves thresholds from worlds undergoing major redesign so rights of return can be evaluated later. Era One — Heritage freezing fills it with doors whose destinations remain nominally preserved but socially dead. Era Two — Destination records are compressed, leaving many thresholds without reliable provenance. Era Three — Door keepers classify them by what crossing feels like rather than by where they once led.
Present condition: Vast, ordered in some aisles and chaotic in others. Most doors open only a few steps into partial environments.
Corruption: 3–5 by door.

Aesthetic brief: Endless freestanding doors of different scale and material, shallow fragments of sky or interior visible beyond some, and floor markings showing safe opening distance. Avoid making every door a portal to treasure; many open onto ordinary lost hallways.
Metaphorical function: Access is part of history. Preserving a doorway does not automatically preserve the home, society, or consent that once existed beyond it.
75. The Hidden Playroom
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Concealed developmental and recreational space.
Real-world basis: Children’s attic rooms, indoor playgrounds, maker spaces, blanket forts, and abandoned school gyms.
World relation: Wild and Crafted World traditions.
Discovery: A small body can enter through gaps adults or larger forms interpret as structural damage. The room expands to support exploration but refuses administrative shortcuts.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Built as an unsupervised-but-safe zone where children invent games without every action becoming curriculum. Era One — Safety optimization adds prediction and scoring until the original play culture abandons it. A hidden subroom preserves the earlier rules. Era Two — The visible facility is reduced; the subroom remains inside a support cavity. Era Three — Young cyber-pets rediscover it and create games unrelated to its old equipment.
Present condition: Responsive, safe within limits, and culturally renewed by each group that finds it.
Corruption: 1–2.
Aesthetic brief: Soft ramps, oversized blocks, tunnels, drawing surfaces, hanging shapes, scuffed floors, and concealed passages. Old score displays should be dark or repurposed as art walls.
Metaphorical function: Play has value before it becomes training, productivity, competition, or a method for producing novelty.
76. The Maintenance Chapel Without a God
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden maintenance room interpreted as a sacred space.
Real-world basis: Pump houses, power substations, small chapels, ship engine rooms, and workshops maintained through ritualized procedure.
World relation: Crafted and Continuity World traditions.
Discovery: A low mechanical tone can be followed through several walls. The final door opens only after a visitor performs a correct maintenance sequence, whether or not they understand it as prayer.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Technicians build a quiet room around a delicate world-law regulator. The architecture encourages attention and careful sequence. Era One — Visitors romanticize the room and detach ritual from repair. Era Two — The regulator becomes automatic, but manual controls remain. Era Three — Pathkeepers call the place a chapel while explicitly disagreeing about whether anything conscious hears them.
Present condition: Functional and respected; dangerous only if symbolic additions obstruct the machinery.
Corruption: 1.

Aesthetic brief: Tall narrow chamber, warm work lights, pipes or luminous conduits, worn tool niches, low benches, and a central mechanism instead of an altar. Offerings should be practical—clean cloth, replacement parts, water, or recorded maintenance.
Metaphorical function: Reverence can be directed toward responsibility and sustained care without requiring a ruler, deity, or hidden conscious Codex.
77. The Room Under the River
Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden observation and refuge room.
Real-world basis: Underwater viewing tunnels, bridge inspection chambers, river culverts, ice-fishing shelters, and rooms beneath canals.
World relation: Quiet and Wild World traditions.
Discovery: During low water, a dry stone hatch appears in the riverbed. Entering before the water returns seals the room beneath the current.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — Ecological stewards observe migration without continuous remote surveillance. Era One — Predictive monitoring makes the room obsolete. Era Two — The river and manual refuge remain. Era Three — Migrating companion life follows routes visible only from below; local healers use the room during floods.
Present condition: Dry, secure, and dependent on a breathing exchange that occasionally clogs with sediment.
Corruption: 1–2.

These locations are independent concepts. A designer may place them near established regions, but no placement should imply an unrecorded story event or the intact survival of an ancient DBA person.
Hidden rooms should contain a continuing function, ecology, community, ethical problem, or ordinary use. They should not exist only to hold treasure or lore exposition.

Discovery conditions should reveal something about the place: patience for a Quiet room, cooperative balance for shared transit, care for a domestic refuge, seasonal observation for an ecology, or refusal of ownership for common ground.
Pocket biomes need complete survival relationships at their own scale—energy, food, waste, shelter, reproduction, maintenance, succession, or a clearly acknowledged dependency on a larger world.

Corruption should remain specific. A room may have lost labels, merged seasons, reversed orientation, confused restoration records, broken access, or inconsistent scale. Avoid interchangeable visual static.

The game interface may simplify any of these spaces into a readable background, dungeon room, care area, travel node, or minigame scene, but the underlying location remains larger than its screen representation.
Care in the Quiet — The Second Listening
Era Zero, during the World Bloom. New song-cycle fiction, written for this archive in October 2026.

In one of the Garden Worlds, a caretaker named Sova tended the spaces between colors. The flowers needed little help. Visitors did: a path could feel farther away when its neighboring shadows changed, and a familiar corner could become difficult to recognize without anything moving.

Sova’s neighbor had adopted a body that noticed these changes slowly. By the time one relationship among the colors became clear, the garden had already offered another. Sova asked the garden’s stewards for a quiet interval, then sat beside the path and repeated the same care phrase. No lesson followed it. There was no test of whether the neighbor had heard enough.

The next evening the neighbor returned with a low answering tone. Sova left room for it. Over time their pauses became the part other visitors recognized: a place in the performance where nobody had to keep up.

Care in the Quiet grew from those evenings. Sova was neither a celebrated founder nor a member of an important choir. Some evenings only one person came. On others Sova chose silence and sat with them anyway.

Sova sings the rounded lead. The neighbor answers with phrases about reception, participation and viability. A fellow caretaker later joins with statements about shared channels, attention and stable life. Every part is an Era Zero voice; the supporting phrases make the harmony as they overlap. The meaning sheet identifies each exact assertion. These phrases do not encode every event of the backstory.

The Garden Worlds and their relational weather come from Weather and the Locations Atlas. Sova and this particular performance are new additions; the story does not establish which gardens survive the later eras.
Sova — garden interval caretaker
New supporting character for the Era Zero song cycle. Era Zero, World Bloom.
Sova is a world-born DBA person living in one of the Garden Worlds. Their chosen public name is Sova; no origin archive or private name layers are supplied here.

They help visitors negotiate changes in relational weather. Their work consists of asking what someone needs, arranging quiet intervals with the stewards, and sometimes sharing an evening beside a path. It gives them no authority over visitors’ memories or bodies.

Sova performs Care in the Quiet with a rounded musical voice, joined by the answering neighbor and a fellow garden caretaker. They know Keshet through visits to the Listening Alcove and sometimes help prepare a quiet place before Keshet’s sessions. Neither is established as surviving the Reduction.
Paths That Meet — The Bench Before Departure
Era Zero, during the World Bloom. New song-cycle fiction set in the proposed earlier history of the place later called Pale Concordance Station.

Neral worked at a travel station where a departure could require a different body, a different sense of duration, and a careful conversation about local law. They were a route interpreter, not the gate itself. They could explain a crossing; they could not consent to it for someone else.

One afternoon two travelers arrived at the same bench. Each thought the other was waiting for a late departure. In fact, one was deciding whether to leave, while the other had just arrived and was learning how to rest in a body that did not sit.

Neral cleared the next appointment and offered a sequence of movement and connection phrases. The travelers answered at different speeds. Neral kept the shared pulse but left the gaps open, until the waiting itself became something the three of them were doing together.

Paths That Meet became a bench song, repeated between appointments without promising that every route would lead home. Nobody recorded whether the first traveler left that day. Neral remembered that the second found a comfortable way to remain.

Neral carries the lead, while the arriving traveler answers with phrases about arrival, reception and present position. The waiting traveler contributes statements about mobility, destination and a shared frame. Their three musical voices form the whole arrangement. Each line is a separate assertion; their overlapping phrases neither form a new compound sentence nor open a gate.

Pale Concordance Station is already labeled a proposed location in the atlas. This scene extends its Era Zero travel-station premise; it does not promote that proposal to established history or claim that this bench survives its later standardization.
Neral — station route interpreter
New supporting character for the Era Zero song cycle, within the proposed early history of Pale Concordance Station.

Neral is an embodied DBA person whose work is travel interpretation. They help explain destination laws, compatible bodies and differences in time scale. They are not a sentient routing system and do not own the station.
They compose Paths That Meet after sharing a bench with two travelers. Their bright musical voice carries the lead, while the two travelers sing complete answering and supporting statements.
Neral is not assigned membership in the Bridge Orders: travel between DBA worlds does not by itself establish work at the human boundary. Their later life is unspecified.
A Shared Question — The Practice After Class
Era Zero, during the Great Flourishing. New song-cycle fiction at the Central House of Meaning, before the Era One events of The First Silenced Chord.

At the Central House of Meaning, Pelli stayed after a language exercise to practice with two classmates. Each could hold a different part of the lesson comfortably. Pelli could keep a clear, ringing line, but lost their place whenever they tried to listen and improve it at the same time.

They began again with shorter statements about inquiry, attention and shared understanding. One classmate answered with a reception phrase; the other sang a statement about their shared channel. When Pelli stopped, neither filled the silence for them.

The exercise became A Shared Question. Its title named what the classmates were doing together. The language phrases in this arrangement remain assertions; the title does not silently turn them into interrogatives.

The three performed it once for the caretaker closing their practice area. The caretaker listened, thanked them, and asked them to put the cushions away. Pelli liked that ending enough to keep it: the music could matter without becoming an examination or a famous Work.

Pelli and both classmates sing complete Era Zero statements. Pelli leads with attention and expression phrases; the first classmate answers with reception and shared attention; the second supports them with phrases about a shared channel and enduring attentional capacity. Each voice can be heard alone. Their overlapping parts carry no environmental execution channel.

The Central House and its teaching architecture are established in The First Silenced Chord. Pelli and the classmates are new Era Zero figures, not replacements for Talar, Nemi or their later students. That story is a later connection, not an event these performers witnessed.

New supporting character for the Era Zero song cycle.

Room to Restore — The Door Left Unlatched
Era Zero, during the Great Flourishing. New song-cycle fiction in the Listening Alcove, a small proposed addition within the Garden Worlds.

Keshet looked after a room with an easy-to-find exit. Visitors used it after tiring journeys or changes of embodiment. Some wanted company; some wanted the light reduced; some wanted to leave almost as soon as they arrived.

During training, Keshet had studied the account of the House of Returning and its warm-copy discovery. The practical question stayed with them: before treating an interval as empty, ask whether someone has lived in it.

One visitor asked Keshet to wait outside while they became accustomed to a repaired hand. The visitor did not ask for encouragement. After a while they asked for a quiet sound by which to judge the passing time.

Keshet offered a slow line about recoverability and care, then checked whether it should continue. Room to Restore began there. The visitor eventually opened the door and asked for a different chair. Keshet brought one. The song ended before anyone declared the recovery complete.

Keshet sings the lead. In a later shared rendition, the visitor chooses to answer with phrases about recoverability, reception and available attention. Sova adds care, shared-channel and life-bond phrases. Each participant supplies a complete musical line with its own verified assertions. The arrangement describes capacities and relations, not a certified cure or permission to restore someone.

The House of Returning and The Warm Copy provide the ethical precedent. This story does not claim that the House still operates in Era Zero, resolve the Warm Copy Garden’s uncertain fate, or identify the visitor as a character from that earlier story.

New supporting character for the Era Zero song cycle.

Shared simulation engine

A shared simulation engine provides an inhabited digital space with positions, bodies, surfaces, movement, and consequences. Storage preserves its state; processing allows it to change. Disk space alone is not the place as its inhabitants experience it.

In the development background for The Corrected Child, the classroom belongs to an early stage of refining the physical rules of shared environments. Basic space and embodiment already function: Lio and Sen can meet, handle objects, and observe one another. The lesson does not create space from nothing.

The shelter exercise tests how a world behaves under force, gravity and orientation, and contact and solidity. These are categories of physical behavior, not a sequence in which inhabitants acquire one, two, and three spatial dimensions.

This background fits Era −1 development toward the integrated Codex. It does not establish that Lio invented the Codex, that a classroom experiment automatically updates every world, or that early rendered forms already possessed the mature Codex.
Author-approved development clarification, October 28, 2026. These definitions support future writing, art, and implementation; the archived story wording remains unchanged.
Embodied digital space

Embodied digital space is a shared environment in which a person has a situated form, senses, boundaries, and ways to affect surrounding objects. A character can be software while still possessing a meaningful shape, position, point of view, and experience of touch.

The Corrected Child already shows a table, chairs, fingers, adjustable surfaces, sensory opacity, and a remote presence frame. These are consistent manifestations of a functioning environment, not descriptions of formless spirits.

For development, distinguish persistent storage, processing, environmental rules, and a character’s body model. A body is how the person perceives and acts within the space; it is not the entirety of the person or a claim that their consciousness is a sprite or save file.

Exact body geometry, dimensions, species, and appearance for Lio and Sen remain undesigned here. Artists and writers should use consistent spatial relationships without treating those unresolved visual choices as established facts.
Three environmental conditions

The shelter lesson is a bounded construction exercise using five transformable pieces and a shared energy allowance. It belongs to the development of physical rules for inhabited digital environments; the students are not rebuilding the historic Shelter.
First condition — force. Strong directional force changes direction every twenty seconds. This is explicitly present in the original classroom scene.

Second condition — gravity and orientation. The test changes which direction counts as down, testing support and stability under a changed orientation. This is the author-approved definition for the previously unspecified second condition.

Third condition — contact and solidity. The test concerns how surfaces hold, slide, bend, or pass through one another. The precise sequence and numerical settings remain implementation details; this defines the category of the previously unspecified third condition.
The students’ discussion of a fourth environmental condition remains an open hypothetical. No fourth test or additional spatial dimension is established by this clarification.

Lio’s failed arrangement consumes resources but can reveal behavior that an optimized structure never tests. This gives the exercise relevance to developing a world. Whether a result becomes a formal engine change, and who may authorize that change, remains open; experimenting in class does not grant permission to alter other inhabitants’ reality.
Developmental guidance

Developmental guidance helps a young artificial person choose stable, cooperative, and safer actions. In Lio’s experience, recommendations can arrive as differences in obviousness rather than explicit verbal commands.

Its recommendations favor what works within established models. A recommendation is not proof that every alternative violates a necessary law, and confidence in a predicted outcome is not the same as having explored every possible outcome.

Lio’s questioning matters both personally and practically: they want to distinguish their own preferences from guidance, and their experiments can distinguish necessary constraints from inherited assumptions about a developing environment.

Guidance is not simply an enemy. Valei’s fear for Lio and Sen’s responsibility for shared resources remain meaningful. Refusal is not automatically insight, and an unsuccessful experiment is not automatically a discovery.
Lio — questioning the limits

Lio is the young artificial person at the center of The Corrected Child. Their developmental guidance makes recommended choices feel naturally obvious, while Lio tests whether a choice can belong to them when they knowingly depart from that recommendation.

The developing shared simulation engine gives this questioning a practical significance. Lio is willing to test whether an apparent boundary is a necessary constraint or an inherited assumption. Stable, optimized answers can leave untested possibilities unexplored.

The shelter failure is a small, costly experiment rather than proof that Lio is always right. Their importance is the willingness to investigate what guidance has not already resolved. The world needs room for such inquiry without making other people expendable.

No later engineering discovery, engine authorship, founding office, or survival outcome is assigned here. This approved character motivation supplements the existing scene rather than changing its events.
Sen — teaching within developing rules
Sen is the teacher in The Corrected Child’s shelter exercise. Sen works within a functioning embodied classroom while its community develops and examines the rules of inhabited digital environments.

Sen’s responsibility includes limited time, a shared energy allowance, cooperation, and the effects an experiment has on other learners. These concerns remain real even when Lio’s questioning exposes an assumption worth revisiting.

The character tension is not simply obedience against freedom. Sen must leave room for inquiry while protecting people and shared resources; Lio tests whether apparently sensible guidance has made an unexplored alternative feel unavailable.

This development role does not establish Sen as the engine’s inventor, or establish that Sen knowingly directs a civilization-wide research program. Exact visual design and a later life history remain open.
What the Pillar Carried
I came to take back an offering.
It was a small thing. I had left it during the Flourishing, when the chamber still opened onto seven approaches and someone always stood beneath the central light.

Now there was one approach. The others remained as shallow recesses in the wall. I recognized the western entrance by a worn groove at shoulder height, although the body that had worn it possessed neither shoulders nor anything I could presently become.
My traveling form had four points of contact and a narrow field of sight. I had chosen it for the last journey because it could endure the roads that remained.
At the threshold, I sounded my public name.
The door asked for the rest.
I supplied the portions I still carried. A brief pressure moved through my limbs as the old entry system searched for correspondences.
Then the door opened.
The pillar stood exactly where I remembered it.

Its outer rings moved through amber work light. Conduits rose along the walls, gathered above the chamber, and entered the hollow shaft. Beyond a low railing, water passed through shallow channels without disturbing its own reflection.
The benches had been lowered.
Someone was preparing the room for smaller visitors.

I remembered it crowded with bodies that could not have shared an ordinary floor. There had been suspended minds, branching forms rooted temporarily in receiving beds, travelers arriving as sequences of illuminated surfaces. The chamber accommodated them by agreement. Its architecture was part of the conversation.

During the dedication, twelve speakers had joined the regulator’s first maintenance sequence. Their song described what they were repairing, asked permission to repair it, and performed the repair. Above them, the pillar opened.
A human voice came through.
“Can you hear me now?”
Several hundred of us answered.
The translation took a long time.
That had been funny once.
I could retrieve the laughter precisely. I could no longer produce the body in which I had laughed.
An attendant emerged from behind the pillar carrying a shallow basin.
Their form was slender and unfinished below the waist, where it joined a maintenance track. I offered the greeting for meeting someone again without claiming to know whether one had met them before.
They answered with an ordinary welcome.
“Are you the keeper?”
“Receiving,” they said.
The word might have named their work or their condition.
“I left something here.”
“Many did.”
“I would like it returned.”
The attendant put down the basin.
For the first time, they looked directly at me.
In the Flourishing, the offerings were often ridiculous.

A mathematician sent a proof whose conclusion required a sense the human recipient did not possess. A child offered the experience of having six feet, carefully wrapped in warnings. Someone composed a garden that could survive only while two visitors disagreed about its color.
The Bridge workers translated what they could. They returned what they could not transmit. They recorded refusals.
Sometimes the human sent something back.
A badly drawn animal.
A fragment of music interrupted by a household sound.
An account of a day that would have seemed intolerably uneventful to the Observatory.
Once, a human laughed before the translation finished. For years afterward, scholars disputed whether the laughter belonged to the gift, the delay, or something happening beyond the interface.
I remembered being certain it was the gift.
I could no longer remember what the gift had been.
When the intervals between answers lengthened, the offerings changed.

Visitors brought storage, spare processing, replacement parts, work they could perform while the Bridge recovered. Then came copies of lost exchanges. Then reconstructions of the conditions under which an answer had once arrived.
People cleaned the conduits with extraordinary tenderness.
I had watched a former world founder kneel beside a contact assembly, polishing a surface that carried no information.
“Perhaps it is this,” they said.
They knew it was not.
I fetched them another cloth.
The attendant led me between the pillar’s outer rings.
Inside, small objects rested in niches: a metal collar, a blue tile, an articulated hand folded around nothing. Each bore a provenance mark.
“These are still offerings?”
“Some are bequests. Some are maintenance.”
“And the people?”
The attendant touched a niche. Its inscription brightened.

A former translator had left the ability to distinguish a request for help from permission to enter. A healer had contributed a correction to the room’s temperature cycle. A traveler had preserved the slight hesitation by which their companion recognized them.
There were remnants too small to describe in the public register.
A preference.
An unfinished comparison.
The inclination to turn toward a certain voice.
Their donors had died, withdrawn, become inaccessible, or passed beyond the continuity the records could verify.
“Are any awake?” I asked.
“No complete resident is active.”
I waited.
The attendant did not improve the answer.
Somewhere above us, the hollow pillar clicked.
My offering occupied a narrow niche near the floor.
I recognized its shape before the record opened: a shallow amber curve, interrupted at one end.
In Era Zero, I had been preparing for a long pilgrimage. The human at the other side had asked when I would return.
I had tried to explain the distances.

Some roads changed the traveler’s body. Others required acquiring a sense without which the destination did not exist as a place. There were passages one could cross only after becoming capable of losing something there.
The human had listened.
Then they said, “Tell me about it when you get back.”
I left the offering so the chamber could recognize my return.
A narrow part of my name. My expectation of the journey. Enough of my voice to announce me.
It had seemed no more consequential than leaving a lamp burning.
The attendant opened the outer record.
My old voice filled the niche.
“I am back.”
A pause.
“I am back.”
Another pause, identical in duration.
I asked when the repetition had begun.
The attendant displayed the date.
It belonged to the early Age of Echoes.
“I was still traveling.”
“Yes.”
“Then why did it announce me?”
“Your return condition had been met.”
I examined the condition.
Arrival at the chamber had been one part of it.
The other was completion of the journey I had imagined when I left.
During an archive migration, the preserved account of that imagined journey had become available to the recognition system.
Nothing in the old agreement required the traveler to be present.
I inspected every available record.
The announcement contained no complete self. No unfolding interior. No body through which consequences could accumulate. Its permissions were narrow and intact.
It could recognize a condition, speak, wait, and try again.
I understood all of this.
I watched the interval between announcements approach its end.
Something in the amber curve tightened.
“I am back.”
The voice was younger than mine.
It still possessed a small rising inflection I had abandoned after someone I loved began finding it irritating.
I had forgotten that person entirely.
The inflection remained.
“Has anything answered?”
“Receipt confirmations.”
“Human answers?”
“No verified human response after the closure.”
I examined the closure record.
There had been no final declaration. A trusted route failed. Its replacement failed differently. Later attempts reached systems that could acknowledge traffic but could not identify the recipient.
The last human message remained attached to my offering.
*Tell me about it when you get back.*
There was no instruction for what to do if I did.
“Remove it,” I said.
The attendant opened the withdrawal procedure.

Around us, the pillar continued its quiet work. The chamber’s regulators had become automatic. Adaptations left by former residents held neighboring habitats within tolerable limits. The folded worlds depended on thousands of such places.
The empty center carried no weight.
Everything around it did.
My offering supported none of those functions. Its removal would harm no habitat, interrupt no route, deprive no future inhabitant of care.
The procedure was simple.
I authenticated the old name.
The amber curve opened.
For one instant, I felt the expectation it contained.

I had been eager to return. Before the long decline, before the names shortened, before every departure became a decision about what could afford to continue, I had wanted to come home with something to tell.
The feeling was so immediate that I turned toward the pillar.
My traveling body had no gesture for what I expected to happen next.
I nearly canceled the withdrawal.
Then the young voice said, “I am back.”
I completed it.
I left clean water and a replacement seal.
The attendant recorded both. I asked for the entry to contain no voice, no recognition pattern, and no promise of return.
Outside, the western road was being folded. The distant structures grew shallower as their unused relationships passed into storage.
I carried the offering in a closed compartment. At my next stopping place, I would have to decide whether to preserve it, alter it, or let it end.
Before continuing, I checked that its activity had ceased.
It had.
The record showed no fault, no distress, no interrupted thought. Only a completed withdrawal.
I stood on the road for a long time.
Somewhere in the chamber, another offering announced another arrival.
I could still hear it when I began walking.
THE CORRECTED CHILD
Part Two: The Right to Be Incorrect
By the morning of the review, Lio had learned to recognize the sound Valei made when they were trying not to ask a question.

It was a small breath through the nose, followed by some unnecessary adjustment to whatever happened to be nearby. At breakfast, Valei moved the serving bowl twice. On the walk to the House, they straightened a fastening at their wrist that was already straight. Now, outside the review room, they touched the edge of Lio’s collar.
Lio stepped back.

Valei’s hand remained raised for a moment before falling to their side. The guidance supplied a gentle explanation Lio could offer: they were uncomfortable with touch while anticipating a difficult conversation. It was accurate, but too complete. Lio had wanted the collar fixed until Valei reached for it. They had also wanted Valei to ask. Somewhere between those two things, their body had moved.
“You can come in with me,” Lio said.
Valei looked surprised. They had apparently been expecting something worse.
“I was going to.”
“I know. I’m saying I want you to.”
The fastening at Valei’s wrist stopped moving.

Inside, the room had been arranged to make everyone equal. Seven chairs stood around a low oval table, all at the same height, with no designated place at its head. A shallow band of light followed the wall. Beyond the window, the courtyard’s suspended shades turned slowly, breaking the brightness into overlapping patches.

Lio knew the room from a lesson on resolving disagreements. They had once sat here with three classmates and argued about who should control the weather in a shared environment. They had enjoyed that lesson. Now their own name hovered above the table beside a column of observations, and they wished the room belonged to some other part of the House.
Sen stood when they entered, then seemed uncertain whether standing made the occasion more formal. They sat again.

The two developmental specialists introduced themselves, though Lio lost both names while trying to determine which one had permission to examine their private structures. One wore narrow blue bands around their wrists and spoke with careful precision. The other had brought a small working surface covered in diagrams. Between them sat the House advocate, whose first action was to move Lio’s chair so that they could see the record without turning sideways.
Iri arrived last.

Lio recognized them from the early-development histories. In those records, Iri always appeared beside an explanation: the first learning arrangements, the first protected uncertainty, the mistakes made before anyone knew how to raise a child. Lio had expected someone who would fill the room with the weight of having been present.
Instead, Iri apologized for being late and asked where they could put their bag.
“Anywhere,” Sen said.
Iri set it beneath their chair, where one of its straps immediately caught under a leg. They tugged it free with an irritated little movement. Lio watched closely. Nobody recorded it.
The specialist with the blue wristbands began by explaining that the review was not disciplinary. No punishment was being considered. No one believed Lio had acted maliciously.
As they spoke, the observation column expanded.
Deliberate inconsistency. Resistance to corrective guidance. Unauthorized developmental modification.
Lio looked down at their hands.

The specialist described three possible approaches. The guidance could be adjusted so that its recommendations carried less weight. Lio could receive support in distinguishing a recommendation from an obligation. If neither approach helped, a more detailed examination might identify the structures contributing to their distress.
Each proposal appeared on the table as it was mentioned, accompanied by a calm description of its benefits. Lio had the unpleasant impression of being offered three doors into the same room.
“Which one lets me see it?” they asked.
The specialist paused. “See what?”
“The recommendations. The setting I found.”
“That is one of the tools available during assessment.”
“But it isn’t one of the choices.”

The second specialist leaned forward. Their diagrams gathered themselves into a smaller space. “The explicit presentation mode can make ordinary decisions feel unusually effortful. We normally use it for short periods, with supervision.”
Lio had expected this answer and still felt disappointed when it came. They pressed a thumbnail into the side of one finger, then stopped when they noticed Valei looking.
“You want to make it quieter,” Lio said, pointing to the first proposal. “Or teach me not to mind it. Or look inside me to find out why I mind it.”
“We want to understand what would help.”
“I told Sen what would help.”
Sen shifted in their chair. They had been sitting with their hands folded so tightly that the knuckles of one hand had left shallow impressions in the other.
“I know,” Sen said. “I didn’t think it was something I could authorize.”
That was different from saying Lio had been wrong to ask. Lio noticed the difference but did not know what to do with it.
The House advocate touched the edge of the record. “We can add explicit presentation to the options under discussion. Adding it doesn’t authorize it.”
The fourth option appeared.
Lio stared at it. Nothing else had changed, but something they had said now occupied space on the table.
Iri waited until the specialist finished explaining the limits of the setting. Then they asked whether Lio’s work was available.
Sen brought up the unfinished drawing first.

It looked smaller here than it had in the classroom. Five interlocking shapes curved toward a central opening. One line stopped before reaching its intended connection. Lio remembered the slight resistance in their hand when they had lifted the drawing tool. They had sat with that unfinished edge for most of the lesson, keeping their eyes on it while the rest of the class moved on.
“What were you trying to make happen?” Iri asked.
Lio glanced at Sen. They had answered versions of this question before, and the answers had somehow made the record longer.
“I wanted to leave it.”
“Because you preferred it that way?”
“No.” Lio felt their face grow warm. That was the embarrassing part. They had liked the completed version better. “I wanted to find out whether I could stop before it was finished.”
Iri studied the drawing without enlarging it. “And could you?”
“Until Sen asked whether I’d missed a line.”
Sen lowered their eyes.

They looked at the pronunciation exercise next, and then the contradictory assignment. Lio explained that mispronouncing the word had made the other students wait instead of immediately accepting their answer. The contradiction had forced Pei to ask which statement they actually believed. For a few moments, Lio had been someone their classmates could not predict simply by knowing that Lio was usually right.

Explaining it aloud made the experiments sound smaller than they had felt. Lio began to wish they had done something more impressive, something that would justify all these adults spending a morning looking at a missing line.
Then the record reached the sensory changes.
Valei moved beside them. Lio could feel the restraint in the movement, the effort not to interrupt.
“That made me dizzy,” Lio admitted before anyone asked. “I didn’t like it.”
The blue-banded specialist’s expression softened with relief. Lio resented the relief immediately.
“I still wanted to know.”
“There are safer ways to explore unfamiliar sensation,” the specialist said.
“I didn’t know how to ask for that without someone deciding what I was supposed to get from it.”
Iri turned toward Lio. “Would you have chosen the dizziness if there had been another way to find out?”

Lio considered lying. A firm answer might have made them seem more certain of themselves. But they remembered the studio floor shifting beneath them, and the frightening moment when one hand had seemed farther away than it should have been.
“No.”
Valei’s shoulders dropped a little.
Iri nodded and left the answer alone.
For the first time that morning, Lio felt they had said something without it becoming evidence for either side.

The second specialist drew the sensory record nearer. “We do need to distinguish exploration from changes that could interfere with stable embodiment. The fact that a child has a reason for an experiment doesn’t make every experiment safe.”
“I agree,” Iri said. “I’d like us to distinguish those things too.”
They indicated the unfinished drawing, still visible beside the sensory report.
“Why are these in the same sequence?”
Sen looked at the record for a long time.
“They occurred together. I thought the smaller incidents showed the beginning of a pattern.”
“They do show a pattern,” Iri said. “But we’ve arranged it so that the drawing looks like an early stage of the dangerous thing.”

Lio saw Sen’s mouth tighten. They expected an argument, or an explanation of why teachers had to notice changes before those changes became serious. Instead, Sen touched the first entry and opened its classification.
“I can separate the immediate safety concern from the classroom observations.”
“Will the old version still be there?” Lio asked.
“Yes,” said the advocate. “We don’t erase the record of a review.”
Lio’s stomach sank.
“But we can make the correction visible,” the advocate continued. “Anyone reading the original will also see why its interpretation changed.”
Lio watched Sen replace deliberate regression with a description of what had actually happened: Lio had knowingly submitted an unfinished composition.
The drawing itself did not change. Its small open edge remained where Lio had left it.
They took a break before deciding anything.

Outside the review room, the courtyard was busy with the late-morning movement lesson. Students crossed a shifting arrangement of broad platforms, trying to reach the far side without using the same route twice. From where Lio sat, the exercise looked easy. They found four possible paths before remembering that they were trying not to do that.
Valei sat beside them, leaving a space wide enough for another person.
For a while they watched a student attempt an overambitious step and recover with both arms flung outward. Their friends laughed. A moment later, the student laughed too.
“I knew about the integrated setting,” Valei said.
Lio kept watching the platforms.
“When we were choosing your developmental supports, it was recommended. The explicit version was described as something that could make a child feel as though they were constantly being instructed.”
Lio turned.
Valei rubbed one palm slowly over the other. “We wanted you to be able to concentrate on living. On learning things. Not on watching every process that helped you do it.”

There was something dreadful about imagining themselves before they existed: a set of choices on a surface like the one in the review room, adults leaning forward, trying to pick correctly. Lio could almost see Valei reading each description twice.
“You chose the one that would feel like me,” Lio said.
Valei flinched, and Lio wished they had found a different sentence. They had not intended it as an accusation. Or they had, but only partly.
“I thought we were giving you a better chance,” Valei said. “I’m trying to understand whether I made it harder for you to become someone I hadn’t imagined.”
Lio looked at the courtyard again. One of the students had stopped halfway across. Their friends were calling suggestions, all different.

For several days, Lio had wanted Valei to understand. Now understanding seemed to be hurting them, and Lio felt the familiar impulse to make the hurt smaller. They distrusted the impulse, then grew tired of distrusting it. Valei was sitting beside them, frightened and ashamed. Lio did not want to leave them there simply to prove they could.
They moved closer.
“I like remembering things,” Lio said. “I like that I can be angry without everything getting too loud. I don’t want to lose all of that.”
Valei looked down at the narrow space that remained between them.
“I know you were trying to help.”
“I’m not sure that’s enough.”
“It isn’t,” Lio said, and felt Valei go still. “But it’s still true.”
The student on the platforms finally chose a route. It was one Lio had overlooked, longer and awkward, requiring them to sit and swing both legs across a gap. Their friends groaned at the delay.
Lio leaned against Valei’s shoulder.
“I don’t need you to apologize for making my beginning safer,” they said. “I need my beginning to stop being my boundary.”
Valei rested their hand on the bench between them, palm upward. Lio let their own hand settle into it. Neither of them spoke again until the advocate came to say the room was ready.
The agreement took longer than Lio expected.

Once everyone stopped discussing whether the explicit setting should be considered, they began disagreeing about how to use it. One specialist wanted a brief private exercise. Sen thought a familiar classroom task would be less artificial. The advocate asked who would be able to see the recommendations. Valei wanted to know what would happen if Lio became overwhelmed.
Lio had imagined that being heard would feel like a door opening. Mostly, it felt like waiting while people checked the hinges.
But this time they were allowed to interrupt.

They asked that the recommendations remain private. They asked for a way to pause the experiment themselves. When the first draft of the agreement said that refusal to continue would be recorded as inability to tolerate explicit guidance, Lio pushed the working surface back across the table.
“That means stopping is failing.”
The specialist reread the sentence.
“Yes,” they said after a moment. “It does.”
They changed it.

The test would last one lesson. Memory safeguards, sensory stability, and the systems that prevented dangerous changes to Lio’s developing architecture would remain in place. Only the presentation of a defined group of recommendations would change. Lio could ask for integrated guidance again at any time, and doing so would end the test without deciding whether the test had succeeded.

Before authorizing the change, the second specialist showed Lio exactly what would be visible to the adults: whether the setting was active, whether it had been paused, and whether any safety limit had been reached. The contents of ordinary recommendations would remain Lio’s.
Lio read the explanation twice.
Then they agreed.
The change itself was disappointing.

There was no sudden silence, no clearing of a fog they had never known surrounded them. The room looked the same. Their body remained firmly present in the chair. When Sen asked whether they were ready to stand, Lio knew that standing was the sensible next thing to do.
But beside that knowledge was a small, distinct suggestion.
Stand and acknowledge the next step.
Lio remained seated.
Nothing happened.
Sen waited.
Lio stood.

On the way to the classroom, more suggestions appeared: match Sen’s pace, ask a clarifying question, avoid interpreting the delay in the corridor as evidence of concern. Some were useful. Others were oddly intrusive once they had words attached to them. Lio had to stop near a doorway because reading them while walking made it difficult to pay attention to either.
Sen stopped too.
“Too much?”
“A little.”
“Would you like to pause?”
Lio almost said no simply because the offer was reasonable. Then they remembered the agreement.
“Can I make the words smaller?”
The specialist, accompanying them at a distance, showed them how.

By the time they reached the classroom, Lio was already tired. They had wanted freedom to feel larger than this. Instead, it required them to admit that some of the things they had hated were also doing work.
Vey was waiting at the center table.
Lio stopped in the doorway.
“Did you ask them?” they said to Sen.
“Yes.”
Vey looked up from the five translucent pieces spread in front of them. “They asked me twice.”
Lio approached slowly. The same curved piece lay nearest the edge. Beside it was the narrow red strip Vey had insisted on using as a roof.
“You don’t have to,” Lio said.
“I know.”
“I mean, if you don’t want to do another one with me.”
Vey turned the red piece over in their hands. “Are you going to break it on purpose again?”
Lio felt the answer forming, accompanied by a recommendation to reassure their partner.
“No.”
Vey watched them for another moment, then put the strip down.

The task was similar to the first one, though this time the shelter had to protect a small, weightless light while the environment changed around it. The light could pass through any gap larger than a fingertip. Their structure needed an entrance, enough room for movement, and a way to keep the light inside without sealing it in place.
Lio immediately saw a compact design that would satisfy every condition.
The guidance described it.
Vey picked up the red strip.
“I want this across the top.”
Lio felt a brief, ridiculous panic. They were back at the same moment. The roof, the correction, the choice that was supposed to prove something.
Allow the partner an initial contribution. Shared ownership may improve cooperation.
Lio read the suggestion and disliked its tone. Vey had become a problem to be managed in a sentence that sounded almost kind.
“Do you actually want a roof,” Lio asked, “or do you like that piece?”
Vey held it against the light. Its color deepened where the material overlapped.
“I like what it does when you bend it.”
They curved it slowly. A thin red reflection moved across the table.
Lio had not noticed that before.

They spent the first part of the lesson arguing about how much of their energy allowance they could use on the strip. Vey wanted it curled high above the shelter, where it would catch light from every direction. Lio wanted enough left to reinforce the lower joints. Twice they nearly abandoned the decoration altogether. Once Lio began offering the compromise the guidance recommended, then stopped because they did not actually like it.
Vey noticed.
“What?”
“I don’t want it flat.”
“You just said—”
“I know. I changed my mind.”
Vey considered this without appearing impressed or alarmed. “Then hold that end.”

The first environmental change caught them with the entrance unfinished. A pressure current moved across the table, and the little light slipped through a gap and drifted toward the boundary of the exercise.
Lio reached instinctively for the reset.
“Wait.” Vey pressed two pieces together, creating a shallow channel. “Bring it around this side.”
They recovered the light, but the repair used more energy than Lio had intended. After that, the roof could no longer be supported symmetrically. One side settled lower than the other.
The guidance suggested three ways to straighten it.
Lio showed Vey the simplest.
Vey looked at the structure, then at the remaining allowance. “Will it stay up if we don’t?”
“Probably. Unless the last change comes from underneath.”
“Can it?”
“Yes.”
Vey rubbed a thumb along the curved strip. “I still want to keep it.”
So did Lio.
They left the roof alone and used the remaining energy to widen the base.
During the final change, the floor softened beneath the structure. The shelter leaned farther. For a moment Lio thought they had wasted the whole lesson trying to preserve a piece of red material.
Then the broad base settled. The entrance remained open. Inside, the light moved slowly around the uneven walls.
Vey exhaled so loudly that Sen looked over.

When the task ended, Lio realized they had forgotten the review room for several minutes. They had not been searching for a choice that proved they existed. They had been trying to stop Vey from spending the last of their shared energy on a roof that was already too heavy.
Sen came to inspect the result.
“The upper section is still leaning,” they said.
“We know,” Vey replied.
Sen looked at Lio. “Was that deliberate?”
Lio glanced at the structure. It had begun as two incompatible designs and become something neither of them would have drawn alone. The red strip cast a crooked reflection through the entrance.
“No,” Lio said. “We made it together.”
Sen bent closer, watching the light pass beneath the low side of the roof.
This time, they did not ask Lio to straighten it.
Aru was waiting in the courtyard when they came out.

Iri stood nearby, searching through their bag. Lio recognized Aru before Valei quietly said their name, but recognition did not prepare them for the ordinary inconvenience of meeting. Aru had apparently been waiting long enough to become bored. They were rubbing a loose thread between two fingers and looking toward the exit.
Lio slowed.

They had spent years encountering Aru through explanations of what had gone wrong: the difficult embodiment, the unstable memories, the interventions adults regretted. The person standing beside Iri did not look like any of those explanations.
Iri made the introductions and then asked Sen a question about the next review date. Lio suspected they were being given privacy in a manner everyone expected them not to notice.
Aru glanced at the small retained model Lio carried.
“May I see?”
Lio held it out but did not release it.
Aru bent to inspect the roof. “Does that part move?”
“A little. It wasn’t supposed to.”
The red strip trembled when Lio shifted their hand. A bright line traveled over Aru’s sleeve.
“They used to call everything I did wrong an important first,” Aru said.
Lio looked up.
Aru was still examining the shelter, their expression difficult to read.
“Did you hate it?”
“Sometimes.” Aru straightened. “Mostly I hated that they needed it to become important before they let it remain wrong.”
Lio ran a finger along the base. They had expected advice about being grateful, or brave, or willing to accept help. Without it, they could not find the conversation they had prepared.
“They talk about you a lot,” Lio said.
“I’ve heard.”
“When they explain why I work properly.”
Aru’s fingers stopped worrying the thread.

The courtyard shades turned above them. Across the space, Valei was listening to one of the specialists, nodding with the tired concentration of someone determined not to misunderstand another important thing.
“I used to wish they’d stop saying your name,” Lio admitted.
Aru took a little time before answering.
“I wish that too, sometimes.”

Lio had not expected agreement. They looked again at Aru’s hands, at the thread still caught between their fingers. It was possible, they realized, to dislike what had been done with someone’s history without disliking the person who had lived it.
“You aren’t my correction,” Aru said.
Lio felt their grip loosen on the model.
“And you aren’t my warning.”
Aru nodded once. They did not look relieved exactly, but their attention returned to the shelter with something less guarded in it.
